new.headline: This is race week, so the plan is short, sharp, and built to put you on the start line fresh. Trust the work you have banked and let the taper do its job.

answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer: No, please skip the 16-miler. A long run this close to race day cannot add fitness, but it can leave your legs flat on Sunday, nick a calf, or chew into the glycogen you want to start the race with. Heavy, flat legs in the last ten days are the single most common taper feeling, and runners who respond by piling on more mileage almost always regret it. Last week you ran 34 miles, including a clean 12-miler with low drift and a tidy 7-rep workout at 8:36/mi; that is a textbook taper week, not a sign of lost fitness. Put the 16 in the bank for your next build and let race day be the hard effort.

new.analysis:
You followed last week's plan exactly: five runs, the 8 with 4 at marathon pace, the short Saturday, and 12 miles on Sunday at 10:00/mi with only +7 bpm of drift. That is a strong taper signal, not a weak one.

The heavy, flat feeling is the taper talking. Blood volume is shifting, muscle glycogen is refilling, and the nervous system is stepping down from weeks of load. The cure is not more miles, it is patience; most runners feel their best legs on Wednesday or Thursday of race week, then oddly sluggish again Friday, then good on Sunday.

Volume drops roughly another 40 percent this week on purpose. We keep a short pickup day midweek with a few marathon-pace minutes to remind the legs of race pace without taxing them, then a true shakeout on Saturday with four strides to open things up.

For race day, 3:45 is 8:35/mi. Aim to run the first 10 miles at 8:40 to 8:45/mi, settle into 8:30 to 8:35/mi through 20, then race what is left. Start fueling gels from mile 4 and take one every 25 to 30 minutes; sip at every aid station. Lay kit out Saturday night, eat a familiar breakfast three hours out, and get to the start early enough that nothing feels rushed.

One last thing: the only job this week is to arrive healthy. If anything feels off in a run, cut it short; no session this week can help you, but a stubborn one can hurt you.
